# How to Choose Perplexity's Sources for Cleaner Answers

> **In short:** Before you ask, open the globe icon in Perplexity's search box and pick where it should look — the open web, or a narrower content type such as Academic or Finance. Choose at the start of a new session, then open the cited sources.

Perplexity is an AI answer engine — think of it as a search box that reads many websites for you and writes a tidy summary with numbered links back to where each fact came from. Perplexity used to call its source choice "Focus"; today the same idea lives behind the globe icon in the search box. Picking the right source before you ask makes the answer sharper and easier to double-check.

## Before you start
- A free Perplexity account (sign up with email, Google, or Apple).
- A web browser, or the Perplexity app on your phone.
- About 5 minutes for the first run-through.
- Optional: a PDF or document you'd like to ask questions about.

## Step 1 — Start a new session
Go to **perplexity.ai** in your browser, or open the Perplexity app, and start with an empty search box. Perplexity calls each conversation a **session**, and the source choice is made at the start of one: Perplexity's help center says you can't switch Focus within a session. If you're in the middle of an older conversation, start a new one first. You'll know it worked when you see an empty search box with no earlier answers above it.

## Step 2 — Open the globe icon and pick your sources
In the search box, look for the **globe icon** and click or tap it. This is where you tell Perplexity where to look. **Web** is the everyday choice — good for general questions, news, and how-tos. Depending on your plan, you may also be able to narrow the search to a content type such as **Academic** (scholarly papers) or **Finance**. Turning **Web** off makes Perplexity answer only from what the AI model already knows, without searching websites — handy for brainstorming, but there will be no fresh sources to check. If an option isn't on your screen, stay with **Web**. 💬 Example: researching a sleep claim → choose **Academic** if you see it. You'll know it worked when your choice stays selected as you start typing your question.

## Step 3 — Type your question the way you'd ask a friend
Click into the search box and write a full, plain-English sentence — not just one or two keywords — then select **Search** and send it. 💬 Example: *"What does recent research say about the effect of screen time on teenagers' sleep?"* You'll know it worked when the answer arrives with small citation numbers next to its sentences.

## Step 4 — Read the sources, not just the summary
Each numbered citation links to a page Perplexity read. Open at least one — especially for anything important — and check that the page really says what the summary claims. Some citations carry a small shield label: **Government**, **Academic**, or **Trusted**. Perplexity's help center explains that the label rates the website, not each individual claim, so it's a hint about the site rather than proof that a sentence is right. You'll know it worked when you can open a citation and find the passage that backs up the sentence next to it.

## Step 5 — Ask follow-ups in the same session
Type your next question in the box below the answer instead of starting over. Perplexity says follow-up questions stay in the same session, so you can refine an answer without repeating yourself. If you keep jumping between unrelated topics, it can lose track — for a brand-new topic, start a new session and pick your sources again. 💬 Example: *"Which of these studies looked at teenagers specifically?"* You'll know it worked when the follow-up answer builds on the first one instead of starting from scratch.

## Step 6 — Ask questions about your own file
Perplexity lets you upload a file to a session, ask questions about it, and search the web in the same session. Attach a PDF or document — a rental agreement, a class syllabus, a long report — and ask about it in plain words. 💬 Example: *"List every date and deadline mentioned in this syllabus."* You'll know it worked when the answer refers to passages from your file and you can find them in the document yourself.

## Common mistakes
- **Changing sources halfway through.** The source choice belongs to the session. If a conversation drifts into a new topic that needs different sources, start a new session instead of fighting the old one.
- **Trusting the summary without opening a source.** AI summaries are usually right, but "usually" isn't "always". Open at least one citation for anything that matters — money, health, legal, school.
- **Reading a shield label as a guarantee.** Government, Academic, and Trusted describe the website. A trusted site can still be quoted out of context, so read the passage itself.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** before a big purchase or a health decision, ask on **Web**, then open two of the citations — you'll quickly see whether the answer rests on solid pages or on a single blog.
- **For your work or business:** when you need to back up a claim in a report or slide deck, choose **Academic** if it's available to you, so the citations already point to papers.
- **If you're just getting started:** stay with **Web** for your first week and make "open one citation" a habit. Try a narrower source type once that feels natural.

## Try it now
Open Perplexity, start a new session, open the globe icon and choose **Academic** if you see it (otherwise keep **Web**), then ask: *"What does research say about whether morning sunlight improves mood?"* Read the answer, then open one of the numbered citations. That single click is the habit that turns a fun AI demo into a trustworthy research tool.
